https://www.politico.eu/article/nato-pla.text: NATO plans to fortify its eastern edge using drones, sensors and artificial intelligence in a massive network designed to spot and help repel a potential Russian attack. Western officials say the alliance is exploring AI-assisted drone operations as part of the broad effort to bolster its defenses. The aim, however, isn’t full autonomy; instead, machines could help to pilot the drones while human operators make the call on what they strike. The approach echoes what Ukraine is already doing. The embattled country is increasingly incorporating AI into its drone operations, but both soldiers and defense tech firms have repeatedly emphasized that humans must remain at the center of the fight, even as the war becomes more robotic. Advertisement Advertisement For NATO, AI-assisted drones would be part of the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative — a digital battlespace network the alliance is building to track threats along its borders with Russia and Belarus, which stretch from northern Finland to the Black Sea. The new concept includes thousands of drones, sensors and satellites linked with AI to detect potential breaches of allied territory and repel attacks as the first line of defense. Conventional military forces, such as tanks, fighter jets and artillery, will remain the backbone. U.S. Army Maj. Ben Schiff, a software operations officer, told Bild — which, like Business Insider and POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network — that both Ukraine and Russia still rely on humans to control drones. While some systems have AI or machine-learning capabilities that allow brief moments of autonomy in flight, piloting is primarily performed by operators on the ground. Schiff said that “the most boring parts of flying”— drones loitering above the battlefield looking for targets — should be automated. But when it comes to deciding what the drone should strike, that’s where a human comes into play. “So the humans are deciding what the drone does, but they don’t necessarily need to take the action of flying it because we don’t have a million pilots. We can’t fly a million drones at the same time,” said Schiff at the U.S. Army Europe and Africa headquarters in Wiesbaden, Germany. Schiff is a product manager for the EFDI Data Backbone, a developing framework designed to help NATO forces detect, classify, share and act on information at speed and scale. The backbone bridges incompatible computer and command systems across multiple allied nations, allowing real-time data to flow from forward-deployed sensors all the way back to headquarters. Advertisement Advertisement The goal is to help NATO move beyond today's linear system — called a "kill chain" — where information moves from the front line back to a decision-maker and then back again to the battlefront to a "kill web," where data from sensors can be rapidly passed to weapons systems and operators. “The value of a drone, sensor or other capability is not determined solely by its individual performance,” said Maj. Matt Blubaugh, a spokesperson for U.S. Army Europe and Africa . “Its effectiveness depends on how well it integrates into the broader operational ecosystem.” Learning from Ukraine Ukraine is already pioneering the integration of AI into military operations. Soldiers observe a drone in the Dnipropetrovsk region of Ukraine on June 14, 2025. | Florent Vergnes/AFP via Getty Images On the battlefield, Ukraine has made significant progress in using AI to support functions like decision-making, drone navigation, terminal guidance and precision, said Andrii Hrytseniuk, the CEO of the Ukrainian state-backed innovation platform Brave1. This spring, Hrytseniuk told Business Insider in Kyiv that more than 200 local companies were developing AI-based components for drones, missiles, radars and other systems. However, they insist machines won’t control drones from start to finish. Wild Hornets, the manufacturer of the popular Sting interceptor drone, also told Business Insider in May that AI will be gradually integrated at almost every stage of flight operations — target detection, identification and, later, terminal guidance. Advertisement Advertisement A spokesperson for the company said humans will still make the final decision on what to strike. Since Russia is constantly changing its tactics, interceptor operators must keep tabs on these changes and make necessary adjustments, they said. As autonomous systems become more common on the battlefield in Ukraine, commanders also told Business Insider that humans need to remain in the loop. Grek, the call sign of a company commander overseeing robots with Ukraine's 21st Unmanned Systems "Kraken" Regiment, said the goal is to “allow people to focus on the tasks where human judgment has the greatest value.” U.S. Army officers stressed that NATO is using the operational environment in Ukraine to inform military planning for a potential future confrontation. “We’re not copying Ukraine,” said Capt. Ronan Sefton. “We’re learning from Ukraine.” The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, The Telegraph, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio. Advertisement Now, the two bands have confined their collaboration, and will be heading across the pond for a series of UK and European tour dates in 2027. The tour kicks off in Ireland with an opening night at Dublin’s 3Arena on March 29, before continuing with UK stops in Glasgow, Manchester, London and Cardiff over the following week. WATCH From there, the European leg starts with a show in Brussels on April 6, and includes further shows in Paris, Hamburg, Berlin, Frankfurt, Prague, Vienna, Copenhagen and more. The tour wraps up in Katowice in Poland on May 7. Paleface Swiss and Vola are supporting for all new dates, and tickets go on sale on Friday (August 28) at 10am CEST/9am BST. Pre-sale tickets go live tomorrow (Wednesday August 26). https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: CHISINAU, Moldova: A flight scheduled to carry Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Norway was ​delayed when authorities closed Moldova's airspace because of a drone incursion, a government spokesperson said Wednesday.Moldovan police said a Russian drone crashed on Tuesday in a sunflower field on the outskirts of a village in Riscani district, which caused four fires to break out but no injuries.On Wednesday, government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici said Moldova had closed its airspace on Tuesday afternoon to protect aircraft flying over the country at the time, delaying three departures, including the one carrying Zelenskyy.Also read: Trump's Air Force One's emergency slide deploys, delays trip to GOP soiree in TexasMoldovan authorities confirmed the drone came down and exploded 160 kilometers (100 miles) from Chișinău International Airport. The airspace restrictions were lifted and Zelenskyy's plane took off later than scheduled.The drone that entered Moldovan airspace on Tuesday crossed into neighboring Romania, a NATO member, where it was tracked through several northeastern counties.The ministry said two F-18 aircraft of the Spanish Air and Space Forces were raised to track its trajectory before it reentered Moldovan airspace.On Wednesday, Moldova's police said explosives experts discovered fragments of the drone that featured a propulsion system and characteristics similar to a Geran-type drone, which Moscow has used extensively in its full-scale war in Ukraine. Investigations identified the point of impact, where an explosion occurred and a crater of considerable size was formed, police said, adding that specialists are continuing investigations to determine the type and mass of the explosive payload. Ukraine neighbors both Romania and Moldova, and since Russia's full invasion in 2022, both countries have reported dozens of drone incidents.

https://www.dw.com/en/who-was-eva-mamlok.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OHWZ The only known remaining photo of resistance fighter Eva Mamlok Image: Familienarchiv Siemsen Advertisement In the history of German resistance to Nazism , some names have become symbols: Sophie Scholl , Claus von Stauffenberg , Dietrich Bonhoeffer and Georg Elser . Yet many others have remained largely forgotten. Among them is Eva Mamlok, a young Jewish woman from Berlin whose acts of defiance began in her teenage years and continued until her murder in a Nazi concentration camp. Now more people will get to know her story as Berlin renames Blücherplatz, a square in the district of Kreuzberg, Eva-Mamlok-Platz on October 16. "Eva Mamlok was a very remarkable person. As a young Jewish woman from Berlin, her spirit of resistance was particularly striking," says cultural researcher Alexandra Weltz-Rombach, who has worked extensively with the historians' network "Gruppe Eva Mamlok." 'Down with Hitler' Eva Mamlok was born on May 6, 1918, into a Jewish family in Berlin. They ran a wholesale wine business, and the family belonged to the vibrant Jewish middle class that formed an important part of Berlin's social and economic life during the Weimar Republic. But Eva came of age just as Germany was descending into dictatorship. When Hitler became chancellor in 1933, she was only 14 years old. She was also a member of the Socialist Workers' Youth (SAJ). Following the suppression of the left-wing political youth organization later that year, she became active in the underground resistance. According to testimony from Inge Berner (1922-2012), the sole survivor of Mamlok's later resistance group, Eva climbed onto the roof of a department store on Blücherplatz as a teenager and painted the slogan "Down with Hitler." "She was caught doing that, though she wasn't arrested at that particular moment — that didn't happen until a year later," notes Weltz-Rombach. Known as the Tietz department store, the building onto which Mamlok wrote her slogan was renamed Hertie after its 'Aryanization' by the Nazis Image: Public Domain Arrested for honoring socialist icons Luxemburg and Liebknecht Eva Mamlok first appeared in official records in November 1934, after she was arrested for taking part in commemorations for socialist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht at Berlin's Friedrichsfelde Cemetery. Authorities determined that the 16-year-old held "hostile views toward the state" and placed her in "protective custody until further notice" — a euphemism the regime used to justify imprisonment without trial. She was sent to the women's concentration camp at Moringen in Lower Saxony, where she remained until May 1935. After her release, she continued her anti-Nazi activities despite the increasing danger, facing persecution both as a political dissident and as a Jew. In these underground circles, she met Pieter Siemsen (1914–2004), and they remained a couple until he emigrated to Argentina in 1937. The only known surviving photograph of Eva comes from his personal archive. She had a daughter, Tana, in 1939. The father's identity is unknown, however. The child was placed in a Jewish orphanage in Berlin and deported in 1942 to the Auschwitz-Birkenau extermination camp, where she was murdered. Meanwhile, because she was Jewish, Eva Mamlok was forced to perform compulsory labor at the Berlin firm F. Butzke Schrauben-Industrie in 1940. There she met other women who shared her opposition to Nazism. Together they formed what later became known as the "Eva Mamlok Group," an informal resistance network of Jewish and non-Jewish women. They distributed anti-Nazi leaflets and wrote slogans critical of Hitler. They also shared banned books. "They were books that are today part of Germany's educational canon," from Thomas Mann to Lion Feuchtwanger , notes Weltz-Rombach. She adds that the fact that the Berlin Central and Regional Library (ZLB), Germany's largest public library, stands on the new Eva-Mamlok-Platz is a fitting symbol of this act of resistance and the importance of books. Mamlok and others in her group were arrested for distributing this forbidden literature. On January 13, 1942, she was deported from Berlin to the Riga Ghetto in occupied Latvia. According to Inge Berner's testimony, Mamlok remained active in the resistance there too. For example, she arranged for a contact still in Berlin to send her a cake with a miniature camera hidden inside it to document persecution in the ghetto. In October 1944, she was sent to the Stutthof Nazi concentration camp, where she died in December of that year. Replacing old symbols of Franco-German hostility Blücherplatz was named after the Prussian field marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, whose most renowned achievement was leading his army against Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. Several places, including streets and parks, have been named after him in Germany. "There is no shortage of Blücher memorial sites," says Weltz-Rombach. "And perhaps it's also time to put an end to this old Franco-German enmity — which is, of course, inherent in the name Blücher, given its Prussian tradition — and to establish, in its place, a different form of remembrance," she adds. The square also happens to be the site of the Carnival of Cultures , a multicultural street festival and parade held every year to celebrate Berlin's global diversity. Role models for a new generation Having first heard about Mamlok when a Stolperstein commemorating her was laid in 2011, Weltz-Rombach has been researching her biography for the past few years. The Berlin-based filmmaker, producer and curator has also been sharing the resistance fighter's story through various projects, including an exhibition in 2024 and a podcast series with young Berliners. Since Eva Mamlok was only a teenager herself when she became politically active, the workshop participants can easily relate to her fate. These teenagers learn about Mamlok's experiences at the actual locations where she was active, helping them imagine what it would be like to be arrested and imprisoned for six months without trial for doing things that normally wouldn't be considered crimes — such as simply expressing an opinion publicly or laying flowers at a commemorative event, explains Weltz-Rombach. "Above all, she is, of course, a role model — an example of how one would like to act oneself, and how courageous one would like to be." Women's "resistance was often of a more everyday nature, rather than planting bombs," notes Weltz-Rombach. Their stories offer examples of "forms of resistance that have only recently received more attention." She mentions, for example, a 2024 exhibition and the launch of a database dedicated to female resistance fighters. Even though many of the eyewitnesses have now died, Weltz-Rombach believes there are still many more of these stories that deserve to be brought into the spotlight: "There are definitely many names we do not know, that are waiting to be further researched." Indians in Berlin are joining calls for accountability over controversial voter list revisions. https://p.dw.com/p/5OMFv Skip next section Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate' 10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 Supreme Court says access to internet fundamental right for children, calls blanket bans 'disproportionate' India's top court declared that access to and use of the internet is a fundamental right of every individual, including children, legal news outlet LiveLaw reported Saturday. It said that a blanket ban on children's internet activity could make them vulnerable to greater risks rather than protect them from online abuse and exploitation . The Supreme Court also issued directions to bolster the processes for detecting and removing child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) from social media and other online platforms, the report said. The court stressed that the right to freedom of speech and expression also incorporates the right to know, receive and impart information and ideas, LiveLaw reported. The two-judge bench described the internet as a "marketplace of ideas, creative expression and information" and said that its value went beyond the material it contains, as it provides opportunities for children in remote areas and those with disabilities. "For many children, particularly in remote areas, it is often the only source of learning and information," the court said, according to LiveLaw . For children with special needs, the internet is often the only platform where they can find company with others like them, the court said. The court acknowledged that the internet, in its current form, poses safety risks to children. But it said that keeping children away from the internet because of failures by platforms and the relevant authorities to detect and remove harmful content would amount to mistaking the victim for the problem, LiveLaw reported. What did the court say on blanket restrictions on internet use for children? The Supreme Court said that a legal ban would not stop children from using the internet, and that they could move to other unregulated platforms. "Any blanket restriction on the access of internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality," LiveLaw cited the court as saying. The Supreme Court called for safeguards to ensure online child safety and the regulation of content accessible to children. It suggested measures such as a "child mode" for social media accounts, LiveLaw said. Saturday's Supreme Court judgement comes amid a global debate on the ban of social media for children over risks from harmful content. Australia declared the world's first social media ban for under-16s last year. France followed suit this summer, before its Constitutional Court blocked the move . The US representatives include Pramila Jayapal, Ilhan Omar, Jim McGovern, Rashida Tlaib, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Jesus Garcia. "As the world's largest democracies, the US and India have an obligation to promote and defend the rights to freedom of assembly and expression," Jayapal wrote on X, sharing a letter addressed to Rubio. The letter alleges a "pattern of repression, wrongful detention, and excessive use of force by security forces" during the student protests in Delhi and other parts of the country. The lawmakers also highlight incidents of "apparent surveillance," saying that they had received reports that the Indian diplomatic missions in the US "hired photographers to surveil protesters on American soil." "These incidents raise particular alarm in light of India's documented pattern of engaging in transnational repression, including through the weaponization of consular services, harassment, intimidation, and physical violence," the letter said. The group urged Rubio to prioritize the issues in his discussion with Indian officials. The US Secretary of State is visiting India early next week, after traveling to Uzbekistan. He is slated to meet Indian foreign minister S Jaishankar in Mumbai. His agenda also shows a trip to Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat. Indian authorities crack down on 'Cockroach' protest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video https://p.dw.com/p/5OLtx Skip next section Student leader Neha Bora released from detention 10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 Student leader Neha Bora released from detention Bora was also detained in early October Image: ANI/IMAGO All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during the latest protest in New Delhi on Friday was released later in the night. Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's top poll official. Speaking to the media after her release, Bora called for Dipke and other protesters to be released, saying that they had been "illegally detained". "They are ordinary citizens demanding accountability and their right to vote. Carrying out such illegal detentions and keeping people at the police station overnight makes no sense at all," Bora said. A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year. Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains. The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is being questioned. The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants." Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP Modi's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy". BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday. Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder." "It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said. https://p.dw.com/p/5OLr3 Skip next section CJP's Dipke arrested after detention — reports 10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 CJP's Dipke arrested after detention — reports The 'Cockroach' movement has called Dipke's detention a 'kidnapping' Image: Rafiq Maqbool/AP Photo/picture alliance Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke has been arrested, following his detention on Friday when he stepped out to participate in a rally he had called in New Delhi, media reports said. Dipke was arrested to ‌prevent a ⁠breach ⁠of the peace and will be taken before a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court later today, news agencies ANI and PTI reported. CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh also said that Dipke had been arrested, adding that he would appear before the SEM court in central Delhi's Mandir Marg at 12 p.m. (630 UTC). Singh claimed that Dipke's lawyers had not met him. The 'Cockroach' movement said early on Saturday that they did not know where their founder had been detained, calling his detention a "kidnapping." "Until now, neither his parents nor his lawyers and not the CJP team have been given any updates about his location," the CJP said on X, as it published a video of CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde asking about Dipke's whereabouts. Dipke was detained publicly on Friday as he left the house in Jhandewalan where he was staying to take part in CJP's 'Lehra Do Tiranga' (Wave the tricolor) protest rally in Connaught Place. Videos of his detention showed the CJP founder being told by a police official that he was being placed under "preventive detention" before he was taken to a police car. Dipke was seen displaying India's flag as police and media personnel surrounded him. Some supporters were seen trying to block the police vehicle from driving away with Dipke. Just hours earlier, a group of Delhi Police officials had visited the 31-year-old at the Jhandewalan residence and served him a notice barring the Friday protest. The Delhi Police had previously reiterated that Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law, which prohibits any form of assembly or protest, was in force in the Connaught Place area. "The manner in which he was picked up from right outside his residence, no information about his whereabouts, and the fact that even his lawyers have been unable to meet him raise serious concerns about due process and fundamental rights," Singh wrote on X. Even after Dipke's detention, hundreds of protesters turned up in Connaught Place defying the heavy security deployment. The protesters were seen waving the Indian national flag as part of the CJP's 'Tricolor' rally. According to police, some 150 protesters were detained during the demonstrations. The fresh protests came after CJP co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to a five-day detention in jail on Wednesday for alleged violation of prohibitory orders and breach of a peace bond after they attempted a demonstration. They too were carrying the Indian tricolor and the flag has since been at the center of CJP's campaign. The Indian flag "belongs to the 1.3 billion people of this country and not the Delhi police. We will wave it where we want!" the movement has said. Dipke, Das and Ranka were earlier detained on October 10 from a plane as they arrived in the capital for a protest march calling for the resignation of India's Chief Election Commionser Gyanesh Kumar over alleged manipulation of voter lists. They were released after nearly 24 hours. The world's largest democracy has seen almost daily protests since the start of October. The youth-led ' Cockroach ' movement, opposition parties, student organizations and civil society members are calling for India's election chief to step down over a sweeping revision of voter rolls that they say benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). On Friday, another protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at a key business district in the heart of Delhi culminated in detentions. CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke was taken away in a police car even before he could get to the protest location. It was the second time that Dipke was detained in less than a week . Reports now say that the 'Cockroach' founder has been arrested following his detention, and is due to appear before a Special Executive Magistrate court today. With protests being prohibited and demonstrations ending in detentions, the stir over accountability and electoral reform has also sparked a debate over the public's right to protest. Meanwhile, a group of Democratic lawmakers in the US have called on Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is visiting India next week, to raise with Indian officials the alleged wrongful detentions and excessive use of force during the student protests in New Delhi and other parts of the country.
